title: Testing Whether Activation Probes Can Distinguish Jailbreak Attempts from Legitimate Edge-Case Requests

original_idea.problem: Activation-based detectors may have high false positive rates on legitimate but unusual requests.
original_idea.direction: Collect 50 edge-case, 50 jailbreak, and 50 benign prompts. Train probe on benign vs jailbreak. Measure FPR on edge cases. Compare to keyword baseline.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If activation detectors have high FPR on professional queries, they cannot be deployed without damaging user experience.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: FPR characterization -> determines practical viability of activation-based safety -> directly affects whether these defenses can be deployed. Addresses a critical production concern.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires activation extraction, probe training, and careful dataset curation (especially edge cases). Intermediate: the data curation for realistic edge cases needs domain knowledge.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: FPR comparison table (activation probe vs keyword filter on edge cases). Clear methodology. Dataset curation is the main challenge.

novelty.reasoning: 'LLM Jailbreak Detection for (Almost) Free!' (EMNLP 2025 Findings) trains probes on intermediate representations for jailbreak detection but does not specifically evaluate FPR on professional edge-case queries. 'ALERT: Zero-shot LLM Jailbreak Detection via Internal Discrepancy Amplification' (arXiv:2601.03600, 2026) uses internal discrepancy signals. Research acknowledges that false positive rates on real-world data may be higher than reported, and edge cases near sensitive topics are recognized as a challenge. However, the specific comparison of activation probes vs. keyword baselines on curated edge-case datasets is not a standard evaluation in existing papers.
